After decades of working with veterans as an Army Social Work Officer, as the Deputy Director for Health Care at the American Legion and at both the Department of Veterans Affairs and Defense, accessing healthcare is a very personal issue. Women veterans should not have options taken away from them. Research studies and data collected by federal and private sectors shows that women veterans are more likely to be diagnosed with posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) , die by suicide  and are victims of domestic violence and homicide at greater rates than their civilian counterparts.  These conditions are often after a traumatic experience, such as sexual assault, abuse, sextortion or other harassment. They face added levels of discrimination and stigma in the job market, affordable housing, and show up less in executive leadership positions while hiring practices still favor males over women who might get pregnant.  Divorce and single parenting is another factor that can complicate their lives and leave them in a vulnerable or disenfranchised state while on active duty or as they transition to civilian life.  
Women veterans should be trusted to make decisions for their own lives. Our country trusted them with our defense and national security, let's trust them now. Let us give them the option to handle their medical conditions in the best way to address any complications, traumas or family status needs. The VA does not discriminate against male sexual health. In the 1990s, there was a lot of discussion as to whether or not to add Viagra to the VA formulary. It was decided to add this drug because veterans deserved to be able to make their own quality of life decisions. Women veterans are deserving of the same opportunity, dignity, and respect for their reproductive health. 
Adding new dependents to the VA pecuniary roles should be the veteran’s decision when they apply for dependent’s pay, or a child becomes eligible for Dependency and Indemnity Compensation, Chapter 35 benefits, VA Child Care Subsidy or care. It should not a decision forced upon them or even the taxpayer who foots the bill for 18-26 years.  Yet, in the meantime, the VA still does not offer adequate childcare programs despite decades of advocacy from the Veteran Service Organizations or adequate levels of dependent compensation. Any changes to female veterans current level of access to family planning choice should be coupled by a reasonable increase to those benefits that would be comparable to a court order of child support.

===== FILE 2516__1.docx =====
After decades of working with veterans as an Army Social Work Officer, as the Deputy Director for Health Care at the American Legion and at both the Department of Veterans Affairs and Defense, accessing healthcare is a very personal issue. Women veterans should not have options taken away from them. Research studies and data collected by federal and private sectors shows that women veterans are more likely to be diagnosed with posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), die by suicide and are victims of domestic violence and homicide at greater rates than their civilian counterparts. These conditions are often after a traumatic experience, such as sexual assault, abuse, sextortion or other harassment. They face added levels of discrimination and stigma in the job market, affordable housing, and show up less in executive leadership positions while hiring practices still favor males over women who might get pregnant. Divorce and single parenting is another factor that can complicate their lives and leave them in a vulnerable or disenfranchised state while on active duty or as they transition to civilian life.  
Women veterans should be trusted to make decisions for their own lives. Our country trusted them with our defense and national security, let's trust them now. Let us give them the option to handle their medical conditions in the best way to address any complications, traumas or family status needs. The VA does not discriminate against male sexual health. In the 1990s, there was a lot of discussion as to whether or not to add Viagra to the VA formulary. It was decided to add this drug because veterans deserved to be able to make their own quality of life decisions. Women veterans are deserving of the same opportunity, dignity, and respect for their reproductive health. 
Adding new dependents to the VA pecuniary roles should be the veteran’s decision when they apply for dependent’s pay, or a child becomes eligible for Dependency and Indemnity Compensation, Chapter 35 benefits, VA Child Care Subsidy or care. It should not a decision forced upon them or even the taxpayer who foots the bill for 18-26 years.  Yet, the VA still does not offer adequate childcare programs despite decades of advocacy from the Veteran Service Organizations or adequate levels of dependent compensation. Any changes to their current level of access to family planning choice should be coupled by a reasonable increase to those benefits that would be comparable to a court order of child support.
